title: Reformulating Pfaffian Quantum Monte Carlo with the Hybrid Monte Carlo formalism
authors: Thomas Hauschild, Lin Wang, Finn L. Temmen, Thomas Luu
abstract: Pfaffian quantum Monte Carlo extends auxiliary field methods to anomalous fermionic Hamiltonians, opening access to pairing systems and Hubbard-Stratonovich decompositions that are unavailable in determinant formulations. We show that this flexibility can be combined with the global updates of Hybrid Monte Carlo (HMC), leading to an algorithm scaling as $\mathcal{O}(N_τL^3)$, similar to its determinant quantum Monte Carlo (DQMC) counterpart without pseudofermions. The central observation is that the molecular dynamics force depends only on the magnitude of the Pfaffian weight, which admits a determinant representation and leads to a simplified force expression. This construction also yields unequal-time Majorana correlators at essentially no additional cost. For interaction kernels with no convenient analytic exponential derivative, we employ a truncated force expansion whose errors are removed by the exact Metropolis accept-reject step. Applied to the interacting Kitaev chain, the method agrees with exact diagonalization and resolves low-energy modes localized at opposite boundaries, together with their increasing overlap near the topological transition. These results establish HMC as an efficient sampling framework for Pfaffian auxiliary-field simulations.
summary: This work introduces a novel combination of Pfaffian Quantum Monte Carlo (PfQMC) with the Hybrid Monte Carlo (HMC) formalism to efficiently simulate anomalous fermionic Hamiltonians. By simplifying the force calculation based on the Pfaffian weight's determinant representation, the method achieves favorable computational scaling. It is successfully applied to the interacting Kitaev chain, confirming its ability to resolve low-energy topological features.
main_problem: The paper addresses the challenge of extending Pfaffian Quantum Monte Carlo (PfQMC) to incorporate the global updates provided by the Hybrid Monte Carlo (HMC) formalism for simulating anomalous fermionic Hamiltonians.
main_result: The authors successfully combine PfQMC with HMC, achieving a computational scaling of O(N_tau L^3) and validating the method on the interacting Kitaev chain, where results agree with exact diagonalization.
method: They utilize the HMC framework, noting that the molecular dynamics force depends only on the magnitude of the Pfaffian weight, which simplifies the force calculation significantly.
model_or_system: The primary model studied is the interacting Kitaev chain, a 1D system of spinless fermions characterized by nearest-neighbor hopping, p-wave pairing, and density interactions. The Hamiltonian includes terms for hopping, pairing, and density-density interactions.
key_observables: Unequal-time Majorana correlators, low-energy excitation modes, and the computational scaling of the simulation time.
important_parameters: The simulation is applied to the Kitaev chain, with key parameters including the hopping term (t), pairing term (Delta), chemical potential (mu), and the interaction strength (V).
main_assumptions: For interaction kernels lacking analytic exponential derivatives, a truncated force expansion is employed, whose errors are corrected by the exact Metropolis accept-reject step.
figures_summary: Figures compare PfQMC–HMC correlators with Exact Diagonalization (ED), demonstrate the runtime scaling (linear in N_tau, cubic in L), and show the acceptance rate dependence on the truncation order (N_cut).
paper_structure: The paper details the theoretical framework for combining PfQMC with HMC, derives the simplified force expression, applies the method to the interacting Kitaev chain, validates the results against ED, and analyzes the scaling and physical observables like Majorana correlators.
why_interesting: The development of an efficient, globally updated sampling technique (HMC) for Pfaffian QMC is crucial for studying complex pairing mechanisms and topological phases in strongly correlated electron systems that are difficult for standard determinant methods.
